questions.prompt: How old is the Earth, in years?
questions.explanation: Dated from the radioactive decay of uranium into lead in meteorites, which formed with the Solar System (Clair Patterson, 1956). The oldest Earth minerals, zircon crystals from Western Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old.

questions.prompt: What is the world's population today?
questions.explanation: About 1 billion around 1800, 4 billion in 1974, 8 billion in late 2022. Growth is slowing: the UN expects a peak a little above 10 billion in the 2080s.

questions.prompt: In what year did World War II end?
questions.explanation: Germany surrendered in May (VE Day, 8 May). Japan followed after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and signed aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September.

questions.prompt: By how much has Earth warmed since pre-industrial times, in °C?
questions.explanation: Measured against 1850–1900. 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 °C; the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C limit refers to a 20-year average. Land warms faster than the oceans, and the Arctic about three to four times faster than the globe.

questions.prompt: Antibiotics work against which of these?
questions.explanation: They hit structures bacteria have and our cells don't, like the cell wall or bacterial ribosomes. Viruses run on our own cells' machinery, so there's nothing to target. Overuse breeds resistant strains.

questions.prompt: Who set out evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species (1859)?
questions.explanation: Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea on his own, and their papers were read together in 1858. Darwin knew nothing of genes: Mendel's work on peas, published in 1866, was ignored until 1900.

questions.prompt: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin, in the late 1700s?
questions.explanation: Cheap coal, a big trade empire and high wages made machines pay first in the cotton mills of northern England. Within a century it had spread to Belgium, the German states and the United States.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's energy comes from fossil fuels, in %?
questions.explanation: Oil first, then coal, then gas. Estimates run from about 77% to 87%, depending on how electricity from wind, solar and nuclear is counted. The share has fallen only slowly since the 1970s: new clean energy has mostly added to demand rather than replaced fossil fuels.

questions.prompt: What is the global average life expectancy at birth, in years?
questions.explanation: Around 1900 it was about 32 years worldwide. Low averages in the past came mostly from child deaths, not from adults dying at 30. Today it ranges from the mid-50s in parts of Africa to about 85 in Japan.

questions.prompt: In what year did World War I begin?
questions.explanation: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo on 28 June. Within six weeks the alliances had pulled in every great power in Europe. Around 10 million soldiers died, and four empires fell: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.

questions.prompt: You put 1,000 in a savings account at 5% a year and leave the interest in. Roughly how much is there after 30 years?
questions.explanation: 1,000 × 1.05³⁰ ≈ 4,322: interest earns interest. Simple interest would give 2,500. Over 60 years the gap becomes the larger part: about 18,680 against 4,000.

questions.prompt: Which country has the largest population?
questions.explanation: It overtook China in 2023, by UN estimates. Both have more than 1.4 billion people, but China's population has been shrinking since 2022.

questions.prompt: What causes Earth's seasons?
options: Earth's distance from the Sun changes
questions.explanation: Earth's axis leans about 23.4°, so each hemisphere takes turns facing the Sun more directly. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every case but wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. You test positive: what is the chance you have it?
questions.explanation: Test 1,000 people: 1 has the disease, and about 50 healthy people are flagged too. So only 1 positive in about 51 is real. Asked this at Harvard Medical School in 1978, most staff and students answered 95%.

questions.prompt: How much CO₂ is in the air today, in parts per million?
questions.explanation: Ice cores show it stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm for 800,000 years. It was about 280 before industrialisation and passed 400 in 2015. Measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958.

questions.prompt: In what year did Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.explanation: Sailing for Spain, he landed in the Bahamas and believed he had reached Asia, hence "Indians". Norse sailors under Leif Erikson had reached Newfoundland about five centuries earlier.

questions.prompt: In what year did the French Revolution begin, with the storming of the Bastille?
questions.explanation: The Bastille, a royal fortress-prison, held only seven prisoners on 14 July. The crowd came for its gunpowder. The date is now France's national day.

questions.prompt: How long ago did Homo sapiens first appear?
questions.explanation: The oldest fossils come from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. Our ancestors spread out of Africa in numbers around 60,000 years ago and met Neanderthals: most people outside Africa carry 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA.

questions.prompt: Around what year did Gutenberg build his printing press?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: Kevin Eng · CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: Movable type already existed in China and Korea. Gutenberg's mix was new: metal type cast in a hand mould, oil-based ink and a screw press. His Bible came off it in the mid-1450s.

questions.prompt: What does a central bank usually do to bring down high inflation?
questions.explanation: Dearer loans mean less borrowing and spending, which cools prices, at the cost of slower growth and often more unemployment. Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve pushed US rates close to 20% in 1980–81 to end the inflation of the 1970s.

questions.prompt: Roughly how old is the universe, in billions of years?
questions.imageCredit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration · CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: Measured from the afterglow of the Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background, mapped by the Planck satellite. The oldest stars we know are only a little younger.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: Sue Ream · CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: On 9 November an East German spokesman wrongly announced that new travel rules applied "immediately". Crowds pushed through the checkpoints that night. Germany reunified less than a year later.

questions.prompt: Which Chinese thinker's teachings on family, ritual and good government shaped East Asia for 2,000 years?
questions.explanation: He lived around 551–479 BC and saw himself as passing on old wisdom, not inventing it. His students collected his sayings in the Analects. For over a thousand years, until 1905, China's civil service exams tested candidates on the classics of his school.

questions.prompt: What does E = mc² say?
questions.explanation: Einstein, 1905. Because c² is enormous, a little mass holds a lot of energy: one gram, fully converted, releases about as much as the Hiroshima bomb. The Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of mass into light every second.

questions.prompt: Which religion has the most followers worldwide?
questions.explanation: About 2.4 billion people, nearly a third of humanity. Islam, with about 2 billion, is growing faster, mostly because Muslims are younger on average and have more children. Pew Research projects the two close to even by 2050.

questions.prompt: What is the leading cause of death worldwide?
questions.explanation: Heart attacks and strokes together kill about 18 million people a year, close to a third of all deaths. Infectious diseases led until the 20th century, and still do in parts of Africa.

questions.prompt: How fast does light travel, in km/s?
questions.explanation: Fast enough to go around Earth about 7.5 times in a second. Since 1983 its value is exact: the metre is defined from it. Ole Rømer first estimated it in 1676 from the timing of Io's eclipses.

questions.prompt: Something doubles every year. How many times bigger is it after 10 years?
questions.explanation: 2¹⁰ = 1,024, which is why a kilobyte was long counted as 1,024 bytes. Ten more doublings make about a million, ten more about a billion: steady doubling outruns intuition fast.

questions.prompt: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun, in days?
questions.explanation: More precisely 365.256 days. The extra quarter of a day is why there is a leap year every four years. Earth covers about 30 km every second along its orbit.

questions.prompt: In what year did India become independent?
questions.explanation: British rule ended at midnight on 14–15 August, and the subcontinent was split into India and Pakistan. Partition uprooted some 15 million people, and hundreds of thousands, perhaps more than a million, died in the violence.

questions.prompt: What share of Earth's surface is covered by oceans, in %?
questions.explanation: The oceans hold about 97% of Earth's water, at an average depth of some 3.7 km. The southern hemisphere is about four-fifths water.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher, a student of Socrates, founded the Academy in Athens?
questions.explanation: Socrates wrote nothing; most of what we know of him comes through these dialogues. The Academy lasted, on and off, for centuries, and Aristotle studied there for twenty years.

questions.prompt: Which is the only human disease ever eradicated worldwide?
questions.explanation: It killed some 300 million people in the 20th century alone. Edward Jenner's cowpox jab of 1796 was the first vaccine: vacca is Latin for cow. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and the WHO declared it gone in 1980.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Soviet Union break up?
questions.explanation: Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and the red flag came down over the Kremlin that night. Its fifteen republics became independent countries, from Estonia to Kazakhstan.

questions.prompt: Which civilisation is credited with the first known writing system?
questions.explanation: Cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay, appeared around 3200 BC, first to keep accounts of grain and livestock. Egyptian hieroglyphs followed soon after.

questions.prompt: In what year was the World Wide Web invented?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee proposed it at CERN in March 1989; the first website went up in 1991 and CERN made it free for all in 1993. The internet underneath it is older, going back to ARPANET in 1969.

questions.prompt: Who made the first powered aeroplane flight, in 1903?
questions.explanation: Orville flew 37 metres in 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December. The bicycle makers from Ohio built their own wind tunnel, and their key idea was control: twisting the wings to roll, as birds do.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Hamlet?
questions.explanation: Written around 1600 and set at Elsinore, Kronborg Castle in Denmark. At about 4,000 lines it is his longest play, and Hamlet has the most lines of any of his characters.

questions.prompt: How many people use the internet?
questions.explanation: About three-quarters of humanity, by the count of the UN's telecoms agency, the ITU, up from about 1 billion in 2005. Some 2.2 billion people are still offline, most of them in low-income countries, where fewer than a quarter are connected.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.imageCredit: NASA · Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. Buzz Aldrin followed him down while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. Twelve people have walked on the Moon, the last in 1972.

questions.prompt: Which gas makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Its two atoms are held by a triple bond, so it barely reacts. Plants can't use it as it is: they rely on soil bacteria or on fertiliser made by the Haber-Bosch process. Oxygen is about 21%.

questions.prompt: What did Fleming discover in 1928?
questions.explanation: He noticed that a mould contaminating one of his dishes had killed the bacteria around it. It took Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, at Oxford, to turn it into a drug, mass-produced in time for D-Day.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Western Roman Empire fall?
questions.explanation: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, a teenager named Romulus Augustulus. The eastern half, Byzantium, lasted almost a thousand years more, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

questions.prompt: Who argued in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) that legislative, executive and judicial power should be separated?
questions.explanation: He took England as his model. The US Constitution of 1787 built the idea in: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, the courts judge by them.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, from the 1500s to the 1860s?
questions.explanation: The estimate of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, built from records of some 36,000 voyages. About 10.7 million survived the crossing, and close to half of them landed in Brazil.

questions.prompt: A price goes up 50%, then down 50%. Compared with where it started, it is:
questions.explanation: 100 becomes 150, and half of 150 is 75. Each percentage applies to the current amount, not the starting one. It's why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover.

questions.prompt: Which country has the largest economy, in US dollars at market exchange rates?
questions.explanation: About 30 trillion dollars, a quarter of the world's total, against about 19 trillion for China. Adjusted for local prices (purchasing power parity), China has been larger since the mid-2010s.

questions.prompt: Which part of the cell produces most of its energy?
questions.explanation: They burn nutrients with oxygen to make ATP, the cell's energy currency. They descend from bacteria taken in by another cell about 2 billion years ago, still carry their own DNA, and you inherit them from your mother only.

questions.prompt: Which countries hold a permanent seat, with a veto, on the UN Security Council?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: James D. Forrester · CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: The main Allied powers of the Second World War. Any one of them can block a resolution. Russia, and the Soviet Union before it, has used the veto most, then the United States. Germany, Japan, India and Brazil have long campaigned for seats of their own.

questions.prompt: Whose improved steam engine, patented in 1769, powered the Industrial Revolution?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: Nicolás Pérez · CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: His separate condenser cut coal use by about three-quarters compared with Thomas Newcomen's older engine. With the industrialist Matthew Boulton he sold engines to mines and mills across Britain. The unit of power is named after him.

questions.prompt: Which ancient Greek poet is credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.explanation: The poems were probably written down around the 700s BC, after generations of oral performance; whether a single poet made them is still debated. The Iliad covers a few weeks of the Trojan War; the Odyssey, one man's ten-year journey home.

questions.prompt: Which language has the most native speakers?
questions.explanation: Nearly a billion native speakers, Spanish coming second. Counting people who speak it as a second language, English has the most speakers overall, about 1.5 billion.

questions.prompt: What mainly causes ocean tides?
questions.explanation: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder than the far side, raising two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day. The Sun adds about half as much; when they line up at new and full moon you get spring tides.

questions.prompt: Most of a tree's dry mass comes from:
options: Water taken up by the roots
questions.explanation: In the 1600s Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a pot for five years: it gained about 74 kg while the soil lost about 60 g. He credited the water. In fact photosynthesis takes carbon from the air, and carbon and oxygen make up most of the wood.

questions.prompt: What is the most abundant element in the universe?
questions.explanation: About three-quarters of ordinary matter by mass, with helium making up most of the rest. Almost all of it formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang; heavier elements were forged later, in stars.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes does a typical human cell have?
questions.explanation: 23 pairs, one set from each parent; the last pair, XX or XY, sets sex. Chimpanzees have 48: our chromosome 2 is two ape chromosomes fused into one.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher wrote "I think, therefore I am"?
questions.explanation: Written in French, "je pense, donc je suis", in the Discourse on the Method (1637). Doubting everything he could, he found one thing he couldn't doubt: that he was doubting. He also gave us x and y coordinates, called Cartesian after him.

questions.prompt: What is Earth's core mainly made of?
questions.explanation: The outer core is liquid metal, and its churning makes Earth's magnetic field. The inner core, hotter than 5,000 °C, stays solid under the pressure. The mantle above is solid rock that flows very slowly; molten rock forms only in pockets near the surface.

questions.prompt: You drop a stone from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it falling after 2 seconds, in m/s?
questions.explanation: Near the ground, gravity adds about 9.8 m/s of speed every second, whatever the mass: astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon to show it. By then the stone has also fallen about 19.6 m.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest ocean?
questions.explanation: It covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the land put together, and holds the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 km deep. Magellan named it for its calm.

questions.prompt: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Begun around 1503 and worked on for years. It became world-famous after Vincenzo Peruggia stole it from the Louvre in 1911; it was missing for two years.

questions.prompt: Which empire, founded by Genghis Khan, became the largest land empire in history?
questions.explanation: At its height in the late 1200s it stretched from Korea to Hungary, about a sixth of the world's land. It put the Silk Road under one rule, and the same trade routes probably carried the Black Death west.

questions.prompt: What share of an atom's mass is in its nucleus?
questions.explanation: A proton or neutron weighs about 1,836 times as much as an electron. Yet the nucleus is tiny: if the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the centre. Matter is mostly empty space by volume, not by mass.

questions.prompt: If prices rise 3% a year, roughly how many years until they double?
questions.explanation: The rule of 70: divide 70 by the yearly rate. It works because the natural log of 2 is about 0.69. The same sum tells you how fast inflation halves what your savings buy.

questions.prompt: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The Sun is about 150 million km away, so you always see it as it was a few minutes ago. Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds.

questions.prompt: Which economist wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776)?
questions.explanation: A Scottish moral philosopher. He argued that the division of labour drives prosperity, with his famous pin factory, and that self-interest in open markets, led as if by an "invisible hand", can serve the common good. The book came out the same year as the American Declaration of Independence.

questions.prompt: What is the world's total GDP, in US dollars per year?
questions.explanation: About 117 trillion dollars, or some 14,000 dollars per person. In 1960 it was about 1.4 trillion, before adjusting for inflation.

questions.prompt: What is absolute zero, in °C?
questions.explanation: Zero on the kelvin scale: the point where matter has the least possible thermal motion. It can be approached but never reached; labs have come within a billionth of a degree. Deep space sits at about 2.7 K.

questions.prompt: Which continent has the most countries?
questions.explanation: 54 countries, all of them UN members, more than a quarter of the world's total. Many of their borders were drawn by European colonial powers in the late 1800s, often straight across peoples and kingdoms.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has sides of 3 and 4. How long is the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: 3² + 4² = 25, Pythagoras' theorem. The 3-4-5 triangle was known to the Babylonians long before him, and builders used a rope with 12 evenly spaced knots to lay out right angles.

questions.prompt: In what year did the Meiji Restoration begin?
questions.explanation: The shogunate fell and power went back to the emperor. Within a generation Japan had railways, a conscript army and a constitution, and in 1905 it defeated Russia.

questions.prompt: How far is the Moon from Earth, in km?
questions.explanation: About 30 Earths side by side. All the other planets would fit in the gap. The Moon drifts away by about 3.8 cm a year, measured by bouncing lasers off mirrors left by Apollo crews.

questions.prompt: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: A tiny fraction of water molecules split into H⁺ and OH⁻ in equal amounts, so it is neutral. Each pH step is a factor of ten. Rain is slightly acidic, around 5.6, from dissolved carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: How tall is Mount Everest, in metres?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: Rdevany · CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: The current figure comes from a joint Chinese and Nepalese survey in 2020. It still rises a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia. Measured from its base on the sea floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller.

questions.prompt: In what year did Muhammad move from Mecca to Medina, year 1 of the Islamic calendar?
questions.explanation: He and his followers left to escape persecution, for the town then called Yathrib. The Islamic calendar is lunar, about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so its months drift through the seasons.

questions.prompt: How far is the nearest star after the Sun, in light-years?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri, a small red dwarf too faint to see without a telescope. At the speed of Voyager 1, the fastest probe we have sent out of the Solar System, the trip would take about 75,000 years.

questions.prompt: Why is the daytime sky blue?
options: Air scatters blue light more than red
The upper air absorbs red and yellow light
questions.explanation: Air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more than long ones: blue several times more than red. At sunset the light crosses much more air, the blue is scattered away, and what reaches you is red and orange. Violet scatters even more, but sunlight has less of it and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

questions.prompt: Which was the first self-governing country to give all women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
questions.explanation: Then a British colony, after petitions led by Kate Sheppard. Women could vote but not stand for parliament until 1919. Finland, in 1906, was the first in Europe, and the first to let women stand.

questions.prompt: Which river carries the most water to the sea?
questions.explanation: About a fifth of all the river water reaching the oceans, more than the next seven rivers combined. Whether it or the Nile is the longest depends on where you place the source.

questions.prompt: Who composed the Fifth Symphony that opens with “da-da-da-dum”?
questions.explanation: First played in Vienna in 1808, when he was already going deaf. In the Second World War the BBC used the opening, because short-short-short-long is V, for victory, in Morse code.

questions.prompt: You roll a die four times. What is the chance of at least one six?
questions.explanation: The chance of no six in four rolls is (5/6)⁴, about 48%; adding 4 × 1/6 overcounts. The Chevalier de Méré made money on this bet in the 1600s; his puzzles led Pascal and Fermat to found probability theory.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Don Quixote?
questions.explanation: Published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, it is often called the first modern novel: an old gentleman who has read too many tales of chivalry sets out to live one. Its author and Shakespeare both died in April 1616.

questions.prompt: How many countries are in the European Union?
questions.explanation: Six countries founded its forerunners in the 1950s: France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux. Croatia joined last, in 2013. The United Kingdom left in 2020, the only member ever to do so.

questions.prompt: In what year was the Battle of Hastings?
questions.explanation: William of Normandy defeated King Harold II, who died on the field, and was crowned on Christmas Day. Norman French reshaped English: beef, pork, court and justice all came in with it.

questions.prompt: What is the largest planet in the Solar System?
questions.explanation: More than twice the mass of all the other planets combined, and about 11 Earths wide. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth. Galileo found its four largest moons in 1610.

questions.prompt: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.imageCredit: Photo: Antoine Taveneaux · CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
questions.explanation: Painted from 1508 to 1512 for Pope Julius II, standing on scaffolding, not lying on his back. He saw himself as a sculptor first, and had already carved the David. The Creation of Adam is one of its panels.

questions.prompt: What do the angles of a triangle add up to, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Euclid proved it around 300 BC from his parallel postulate. On a curved surface it fails: a triangle on a globe, with one corner at the North Pole and two on the equator, can have three right angles.

questions.prompt: How many member states does the United Nations have?
questions.explanation: 51 countries founded it, at a conference in San Francisco. The newest member is South Sudan, in 2011. The Holy See and Palestine take part as non-member observer states.
